profile.a: Group 10 (five members) for New Venture Finance.
An early-stage investor with £150,000 to place across three ventures.
The value of Alpha (an energy company), Beta (a medical device company) and Gamma (a firm in a UK market of about £900m), and how to split the money.
Handed in on 13 February 2025; every venture is valued on an exit five years out.
UK ventures; Gamma's market is UK-wide, Beta serves 76 customers globally.
Each venture asks a price per share; the investor needs to know whether the future exit, after the required return and later dilution, justifies it.
The venture capital method: exit value from revenue and EBITDA multiples, discounted at 20%, 30% and 45%, then reduced for future dilution; scenarios on market share; returns at 3x, 5x and 10x exits.

Beta year-5 revenue x 4.5 / EBITDA x 10.2

Gamma return to angel investors vs 45% target

charts.title: Price asked vs value under the VC method (£m)
charts.takeaway: On the team's own numbers all three are under-priced, Alpha by about 2.5 times. A gap that large is a signal to test the inputs, which the paper does not do.

charts.title: How Alpha's value is built (£m)
charts.takeaway: Discounting removes 60% of the exit value; dilution barely matters for Alpha. The answer is driven almost entirely by the exit multiple and the 20% rate.

charts.title: Risk priced into each venture (%)
charts.takeaway: Beta and Gamma are penalised twice, through a higher rate and heavy dilution. Each rate is chosen separately, so the ranking depends on those choices.

charts.title: Gamma: value depends on market share (£m)
charts.takeaway: Each point of market share is worth about £7.4m today, so Gamma's case rests on one assumption. Note: 3.7% growth on £900m gives about £1.08bn in five years, not the £1.3bn used.

charts.title: Investor proceeds at different exit multiples (£m)
charts.takeaway: Gamma pays most if it exits well, Alpha least, which is the trade-off behind the final split.

charts.title: Recommended allocation of £150,000
charts.takeaway: The largest stake goes to the lowest-return, lowest-risk venture: a defensive portfolio that accepts less upside for less dilution risk.
